stories.title: Renewable energy in NI reaches record level
stories.summary: More than half (53%) of Northern Ireland's electricity came from renewable sources in the year to June – beating the 51% level previously set in 2022. And for the first time renewable generation has consistently exceeded non-renewable generation since January. Even when imported electricity was taken into account, the amount of renewables equalled the previous record of 50%, set in 2022/23. The Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald said the increasing level of renewable energy would help Northern Ireland "move away from price volatility and towards more stable and fairer prices". Almost three-quarters (74%) of renewable electricity came from wind. anaerobic digestion, incineration and fermentation – provided just under one-fifth (18%). Solar energy provided 6%, landfill gas provided 1%, and hydro/tidal generation provided 1%. Northern Ireland has a target of generating 80% of electricity from renewable sources by 2030. The increase to 53% to June 2026 follows several years of reduced renewable generation. Lower levels can be due to weather conditions. There is also a high rate of dispatch down in Northern Ireland – when turbines are switched off because there is not enough demand for the power being generated. That is to protect the grid which has a limit on the amount of renewable energy it can carry due to fluctuations.

stories.title: Officer to combat homes pumping sewage into rivers
stories.summary: A dedicated officer is to be hired in west London in a trial to combat the problem of water-polluting misconnections. Owing to incorrect plumbing, affected households pump waste into surface drains, which can then spread, killing wildlife and damaging waterways. Misconnections are illegal, and fixing them is the responsibility of the property owner, external. Local authorities can take enforcement action, and if the pilot - funded by the mayor of London's office - is successful, the measure could be rolled out across the capital. Funding is to be spent where the issue is considered a particular problem, including the River Brent catchment area. Founder of the volunteer group Clean Up the River Brent (CURB), Ben Morris, said there was "good reason" to think misconnections "are the biggest single cause of pollution in London's rivers". He added: "We need to see stronger action from the councils to get this done. "They have the power of enforcement and they need to be using those powers to get those property owners to sort out the misconnections." An information request to Thames Water by the charity Friends of the River Crane Environment (FORCE ) revealed that in October 2024 seven blocks of flats in north and west London were identified as having misconnections. FORCE said this meant at least 100 homes were flushing waste into the rivers Crane and Brent. Since then, only three of the seven blocks' misconnections have been resolved, according to Thames Water. The company said two of the housing developments still pumping out sewage were in the borough of Barnet, while two were in the borough of Harrow.

stories.title: Japan US battering ram against China — presidential adviser
stories.summary: VLADIVOSTOK, September 4. The United States uses Japan as a battering ram against China, Anton Kobyakov, an adviser to the Russian president and executive secretary of the Eastern Economic Forum organizing committee, said at a press briefing following the forum. "However, everyone understands that Japan is a US battering ram against China," he said. Kobyakov noted that as many as four military blocs had been created in the region.

stories.title: Court grants Malaysia ex-PM Najib and son stay of bankruptcy proceedings
stories.summary: Najib and Nazifuddin are disputing the tax assessment in two SCIT proceedings.
article_sentences: The Court of Appeal allowed Najib Razak and his son Mohd Nazifuddin to stay bankruptcy proceedings over unpaid tax arrears of RM1.69 billion and RM37.6 million.
The court ruled the Judicial Commissioner's dismissal of their stay was wrong, as bankruptcy has irreversible consequences beyond monetary loss.
The stay will last until the appeal before the Special Commissioner of Income Tax is resolved, with no prejudice to the government.
Najib Razak and his son.
Mohd Nazifuddin have succeeded in their appeal to stay bankruptcy proceedings against them over failure to settle tax arrears amounting to billions of ringgit.
A three-judge panel chaired by Justice Alwipa Abdul Wahab unanimously allowed the stay application by Najib and Nazifuddin in the decision on Sept 4.
Other judges on the panel were Justices Shahnaz Sulaiman and Ong Chee Kwan.

Alwipa, who read the decision, said the learned Judicial Commissioner (JC) who dismissed Najib and Nazifuddin’s stay application had erred when he held that the appellants suffer no irreparable harm on the basis of Section 111 of the Income Tax Act (ITA) 1967.
Section 111 guarantees a refund of any tax overpaid, should the appeal by Najib and Nazifuddin before the Special Commissioner of Income Tax (SCIT) on their tax arrears succeed.
“We concede with the appellants’ submission that the JC’s reasoning is only confined to the recoverability of money.
It does not and cannot address the distinct and irreversible consequences of an adjudication of bankruptcy as alluded to above.
“The learned JC’s equation of irreparable harm with mere monetary loss was a misdirection,” Alwipa said.

stories.title: Is a whale fossil the leftovers of a Bronze Age Sunday roast?
stories.summary: The head of a whale, believed to date back to the Bronze Age, has been discovered buried on a beach in Islandmagee. A 10-year-old boy was out looking for fossils along the shore when he spotted the back of the skull protruding from a bank of earth - but could the fossil be the remnants of a prehistoric Sunday roast? The find has been described as a totally unique, with geologists and marine specialists trying to establish the fossil's story and the Natural History Museum in London helping to identify it. It was found on the same beach where Ireland's only dinosaur bones were discovered in the late 19th Century and the 1980s. Ten-year-old George was out on a walk at Portmuck Harbour with his parents when he spotted something unusual. "It was just the weird patterns on it," he told BBC News NI. "The bits that stuck out, it just didn't look like a rock. I thought it was a bone, but I just wasn't too sure. So I asked my dad and he said it was definitely a fossil." This fossilised hunk of whale bone has lain hidden in the earth on Portmuck Beach for possibly millennia. Only the back of the head was visible to George, invisible for centuries was the beak, which was about a foot long when excavated. Katy McMonagle, one of the archaeologists who dug the whale head out, said the fossil was difficult to move and very heavy.

stories.title: Indonesia’s top rights body calls for police to probe food poisoning of about 2,000 students
stories.summary: As at Sept 1, 50,000 individuals had been affected by food poisoning cases, a lawmaker said.
article_sentences: Indonesia’s top human rights body urged the police on Sept 4 to investigate several new outbreaks of food poisoning linked to President Prabowo Subianto’s flagship programme to provide free meals to students, which made 2,000 people sick this week.

In separate cases across at least two major Indonesian islands, around 2,000 students and teachers fell ill after eating lunch issued by the government as part of a scheme to eradicate malnutrition launched by Prabowo in 2025.
“Rights to food, especially safe-to-consume food, are human rights,” the Indonesian independent rights body, known as Komnas HAM, said in a statement.
“Without a rigorous sanitation standard...
the nutrition intervention that the state is doing will lose its moral legitimacy,” it said.
Komnas HAM called on the police to launch a probe into the poisoning cases, without providing further details.
The National.
Police did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Komnas HAM also called on the National Nutrition Agency, which oversees the programme, to suspend the kitchens allegedly responsible for the poisoning outbreaks.

Some 170 students and teachers in the South Sulawesi region of Tana Toraja also fell ill after eating the free meals on Sept 3, local media Kompas reported, following more than 1,700 cases spread across the provinces of Central Java, East Java and West Sumatra.
The overseeing agency was slated to hold a press conference on Sept 4, but delayed it without providing a reason or a rescheduled time.
It did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but agency head Sudaryono said on Sept 3 that the poisoning cases would be handled seriously.
